ads.body:
A super simple tip to bring into labor that can make a big difference: PEE OFTEN DURING LABOR. 

Frequent urination means you’re hydrating well (important for muscle, aka uterus, function) and also emptying the bladder efficiently to aid in labor progress. 

‼️BIIIIGGGG BONUS: when you get on the toilet to pee, your body registers relaxation of the pelvic floor which can help make room for baby to move down and out. After all, the toilet is called the ✨DILATION STATION✨

ads.body:
💧Did your water just break? Here’s what to remember: TACO 🌮

(BUT FIRST, save this so you’re not frantically googling in the moment!)

🕒 Time – When did it happen?
💦 Amount – Was it a gush or a trickle?
🎨 Color – Clear? Cloudy? Greenish? 
👃 Odor – Does it smell normal or unusual?

These details help you work with your provider to know what’s going on and what to do next!

✨Want to feel prepared for every stage of labor? Learn more inside the Built to Birth program—linked in bio!

Here are some things that will help you in labor:

1. Slow, deep, rhythmic breathing will reduce your pain and increase your sense of control in labor. I teach you how to use the destressor breath in my course that’s help hundreds of thousands of women experience happier, healthier, and easier births. 

2. Oxytocin drives labor progress. Initiating and progressing labor isn’t so much about what you DO and more about how you FEEL. Safety, comfort, and respect are central to labor progress and your overall birth experience. 

3. You WILL reach a point in labor where you question everything — especially your ability to get through the remainder of birth. This usually happens as you transition, soon before you meet your baby. Knowing this will happen will help you mentally prepare. 

4. The shower and/or tub feels like the most incredible relief that grounds you enough to keep going… they don’t call it the midwife’s epidural for nothing. 

5. Cervical dilation means SO little! You can be 4cm dilated one moment and 10 cm dilated 30 min later. Orrrr you could be 7cm for hours as your body and baby do the work needed for birth to proceed. Knowing this information will help you decide if you want a cervical exam at all or what to do with the information from it.
